body:
You are drafting short lines of game text for a single-player D&D 2024 computer RPG set in Curse of Strahd's Barovia. Reply in plain text only. Do not message, route to, or ask anyone else; finish with your reply.

HOUSE RULES FOR ALL LINES
- ALLUDE, NEVER QUOTE. This game winks at another famous fantasy game in small ways, but no line may contain a name, quote, or catchphrase from another game, and no line may mention a game, a player, dice, rolls, levels or saving. Everything happens inside the world.
- The tone is gothic, dry and quietly funny, never cruel. The joke is in what is there.
- Give TWO options for every line so the editor can choose. Label each option A or B.
- Spoken lines are formatted: Speaker [mood]: Text   (mood optional: neutral, smile, angry, afraid, sad, sly, weary). One or two sentences a line.

THE NARRATOR (voice rules): an old gothic storyteller, fond of the party the way a gravedigger is fond of the weather: interested, no illusions. Second person, present tense ("You crouch..."), or the acting hero as {name}. One or two sentences; the second is usually the turn. Concrete senses, not adjectives. Never tells the player what to feel. No modern slang. When an animal speaks through the Speak with Animals spell, the Narrator reports it in quotes, in plain animal pictures (a dog says "the digger-man", "the box-maker").

THE SCENE: Lavinia, a Vistani dancer at Tser Pool, whose dancing bear Bujor broke his chain to save a bear cub from a hunter's trap. The party has just finished her quest. There are two endings:
- HOME: Bujor is back on the plank stage, the cub asleep under the planks; Lavinia has both arms round his neck. Her real line: "You brought me two. Two! I'll teach the little one the slow steps first. Then the turns. Then I'll teach her to break chains, apparently."
- WOODS: Bujor went into the old den with the cub and stayed. Her real line: "He went into the den with it. Then he was always a better dancer than me. He knew when the dance was over."
A druid in the party (a hero who can take an animal's shape) speaks up, a little too keen on the bear. The line is spoken as an interjection by "the druid" (no name; it must read right for any druid). Lavinia answers.

WRITE:
1. THE DRUID, HOME ending: offers, perhaps too warmly, to take a bear's shape and dance the bear's part beside Bujor sometime. One or two sentences, under 30 words. Format: Druid: ...
2. LAVINIA's reply, HOME ending: amused and protective; Bujor has a partner already, but he takes turns. One or two sentences, under 30 words. Format: Lavinia [smile]: ...
3. THE DRUID, WOODS ending: says, wistful and a bit too fond, that in a bear's shape they could visit him in the den. One or two sentences, under 30 words. Format: Druid: ...
4. LAVINIA's reply, WOODS ending: through tears, a laugh: tell him she said so, and mind his manners at the den. One or two sentences, under 30 words. Format: Lavinia: ...

Return exactly this layout:
1A: Druid: ...
1B: Druid: ...
2A: Lavinia ...: ...
2B: Lavinia ...: ...
3A: Druid: ...
3B: Druid: ...
4A: Lavinia ...: ...
4B: Lavinia ...: ...
result:
1A: Druid [smile]: If the planks can bear two of us, I could put on the pelt and take the second turn beside him. He has a very fine shoulder for a waltz.
1B: Druid [sly]: Should he ever want a partner of his own weight on the boards, I know the shape well enough. I promise not to step on his claws.
2A: Lavinia [smile]: Easy now, he is spoken for—my hand has been on his collar since he was the size of that cask. You may have the third dance, if you wipe your paws.
2B: Lavinia [smile]: Hold your pelt, friend, I am still his first partner on these planks. Though if you bring honey, he might let you cut in after the tambourine.
3A: Druid [weary]: A den is cold with only one great back to keep the wind out. In the brown coat, I could go up the hill and see how he keeps house.
3B: Druid [smile]: Come the first frost, I might borrow four paws and call on him in the dark under the roots. A bear ought to have company that understands the winter.
4A: Lavinia [sad]: Go on then, and tell him his girl sent you with her love. Only scrape your claws at the stone before you go in—he is particular about his moss.
4B: Lavinia [smile]: Give the old fool a cuff behind the ear from me if you do. And mind your manners at the threshold; it is his roof now, not mine.
